R01-C-01: Two drivers leave the same party, each having had one drink too many, and each drives home along the same dark road with the same degree of carelessness. The first arrives home without incident; the second, rounding a bend, strikes a child who has run into the road. Most people judge the second driver far more harshly than the first: he may face prison, while the first, if caught at all, will pay a fine, and the second driver himself will probably carry a burden of guilt that the first never feels. Yet the only difference between them is something neither of them controlled, namely whether a child happened to be on the road at that moment. Philosophers call this resultant moral luck, and it presents a genuine puzzle. A widely held principle says that we should be blamed only for what lies within our control. If that principle is right, the two drivers deserve exactly the same blame, since their choices, their states of mind and their recklessness were identical. Our differing reactions must then be a mistake, an emotional response to a dreadful outcome that we wrongly dress up as a moral judgement. On this view, the honest course is to blame both drivers equally, and severely, for the risk each of them imposed on others. This conclusion is tidy, but I think it is too quick, because it treats our responses to outcomes as noise to be filtered out when they may be tracking something real. The second driver has done something the first has not: he has killed a child. His relationship to the child's family, to the world and to his own past is altered in a way that the first driver's is not. To feel and to judge that he must answer for this is not simply to confuse bad luck with bad character. It reflects the fact that agency extends into the world, and that what we are responsible for includes, in part, what our actions actually bring about. None of this licenses the opposite error of treating the lucky driver as blameless. He did something seriously wrong, and the fact that his drive ended well is no credit to him. The point is narrower: the control principle captures one important strand of our thinking about blame, the strand concerned with assessing character and choice, but it is not the whole of moral life. A theory that cannot make sense of why the second driver should apologise to the family, and why the first has no one to apologise to, has not purified our moral concepts; it has impoverished them.
R01-C-02: Most moral theories divide actions into three kinds: those we are required to do, those we are forbidden to do, and those that are merely permitted, yet ordinary moral thought seems to need a fourth. When a passer-by plunges into a freezing river to rescue a stranger, we do not say that she merely did something permitted, as though her act ranked alongside choosing tea over coffee. Nor do we say that she did her duty, for we would not have condemned her had she stayed on the riverbank and called for help. We say instead that she went beyond what duty asked. Acts of this kind are called supererogatory, and their existence has proved surprisingly awkward for theories that try to derive the whole of morality from a single principle. The difficulty is sharpest for a simple form of consequentialism, the view that we are always required to do whatever produces the best outcome. On that view there is no room above duty, because the best available act is always the required one. If plunging into the river was the best thing she could do, she was obliged to do it; if it was not, she acted wrongly. Heroism disappears into ordinary obligation, and the person who fails to be a hero becomes a wrongdoer. Many critics take this to be a decisive objection: a theory that makes sainthood compulsory has misunderstood what morality is for. Defenders reply that the objection confuses two questions: what one ought to do and what one may be blamed for not doing. Perhaps we should not blame the bystander who stays on the riverbank, since blaming people for failing to be heroes would be useless or cruel, while still holding that the rescue was what she ought to have done. This move is ingenious, and it does capture something; our reluctance to blame is partly practical. But it leaves the rescuer's own understanding of her act unexplained, for people who perform such acts often say, sincerely, that they had no choice, yet they rarely say that those who held back did wrong. Their sense of being called is personal, not a verdict on everyone. What this suggests is that the space beyond duty is real but has a peculiar shape. It is not a zone of optional extras to which morality is indifferent, since such acts are admired precisely as moral achievements. Nor is it simply duty under a gentler name. It is the region where morality stops issuing demands to everyone and starts issuing invitations to particular people, and a theory that can speak only in demands will always misdescribe it.
R01-C-03: A promise is an odd moral instrument. By uttering a few words, I create an obligation that did not exist a moment before, and I hand you a kind of authority over my future conduct. Because the obligation is self-made, it can seem absolute: having bound myself freely, I have no one to blame but myself if keeping my word turns out to be inconvenient. Much of the value of promising depends on this firmness. A promise that dissolved whenever the promiser found something better to do would offer the person relying on it nothing that a statement of intention does not already provide. Yet no one seriously believes that every promise binds whatever happens. If I promise to meet you for lunch and, on the way, come upon an injured cyclist who needs to be taken to hospital, I should miss the lunch, and you would think less of me if I did not. The usual explanation is that the promise was outweighed: the duty to help the cyclist was simply stronger. But this explanation, though natural, misses something. It implies that I had two competing obligations and chose the heavier, leaving me in your debt for the one I failed to honour. In fact, most people would say that I owe you an explanation, perhaps an apology for your wasted time, but not compensation, and certainly not a confession of wrongdoing. A better account starts from what was actually exchanged. When you accepted my promise, you did not acquire a right to my presence at lunch under every conceivable circumstance; you acquired a right against my changing my mind for reasons of my own convenience. Promises carry an implicit understanding of the conditions under which they were made, and both parties know, without saying so, that some emergencies fall outside it. On this view the cyclist does not outweigh the promise; he reveals that the promise never extended so far. This account has a cost, and it should be admitted. If the scope of a promise is set by unspoken understandings, then a promiser who wants to escape can always claim that his circumstances fell outside what was understood. The firmness that made promising valuable seems to leak away. The answer is that the implicit conditions are not whatever the promiser privately had in mind; they are what a reasonable person in the promisee's position would have taken them to be. That standard will not settle every case, but it keeps the exceptions public, and a promise whose limits are public remains a promise worth having.
R01-C-04: Moral philosophers argue with cases. A theory is proposed, someone describes a situation in which the theory delivers a verdict that strikes nearly everyone as monstrous, and the theory is revised or abandoned. The practice treats our considered reactions to cases, usually called intuitions, as something like data: not infallible, but weighty enough that a principle which contradicts too many of them loses its claim on us. Critics have long found this method suspicious. Intuitions, they point out, are the residue of upbringing, culture and evolutionary pressures that had nothing to do with tracking moral truth. To test theories against them is to test a map against the traveller's prejudices about where the roads ought to go. The objection has force, but it proves less than it seems to. Every method of inquiry begins with some judgements it does not, at that moment, question; the empirical sciences rely on perceptual reports whose reliability can be checked only by further perception. The question is not whether intuitions have causes unrelated to truth, for every belief has causes, but whether we have specific reason to think a particular intuition distorted. Sometimes we do. An intuition that tracks a vivid feature of a case, such as whether harm is done with one's own hands, while ignoring features that on reflection seem to matter more, such as how much harm is done, earns suspicion. But suspicion of that kind is itself grounded in other intuitions, about which features matter and which do not. This is why the familiar picture of intuitions as raw data against which theories are tested is misleading in the other direction as well. The method that actually operates is one of mutual adjustment. Principles are revised in the light of judgements about cases, and judgements about cases are revised in the light of principles that have earned our confidence elsewhere. Neither level has final authority, and the goal is a state in which the two support each other. Critics sometimes say that this is circular, and in a sense it is; but the circle is wide, and it is not obvious that any inquiry into how we should live could proceed in a straight line. What follows is a modest but not trivial conclusion. Intuitions are neither oracles nor noise. The debunker who dismisses them all owes us an account of the standpoint from which the dismissal is made, and it is hard to find one that does not rely on some judgement of the same kind. The defender who treats them as data owes us something too: a willingness to let a strong theory overturn a widely shared reaction, as moral thought has done before, when the reaction turns out to rest on a feature of cases that should never have mattered.
R01-C-05: It is often said that forgiveness must be earned. On this view, the wrongdoer must first acknowledge what he did, express remorse and, where possible, make amends; only then is the victim in a position to forgive, and to forgive earlier would be to excuse the wrong or to collude in pretending that it did not matter. The view has an attractive moral seriousness. It refuses to let forgiveness become a soft word for forgetting, and it insists that wrongs make demands on the people who commit them. But the view also has an awkward consequence, for it puts the victim's moral recovery in the hands of the person who harmed her. A woman wronged by a former friend who has since died, or who simply refuses to admit anything, would on this account be permanently barred from forgiving. She could stop thinking about the wrong, or decide that it no longer troubled her, but she could not forgive, because the conditions for forgiveness depend on someone else's change of heart. It is strange to make one of the most personal acts a person can perform conditional on the cooperation of the one person least likely to give it. A better account distinguishes between what forgiveness is and what makes it fitting. To forgive is to give up resentment and the claim to repayment while continuing to judge that the act was wrong. Understood in this way, forgiveness does not excuse anything, since the judgement of wrong remains in place. What an apology does is make forgiveness easier and, often, more appropriate, because it removes the reason that resentment had for persisting: the wrongdoer who sincerely apologises has, in effect, joined the victim in condemning what he did. Without an apology, forgiveness remains possible, but it is a gift rather than a response, and it is offered for the victim's reasons rather than the wrongdoer's. This is not to say that unconditional forgiveness is always admirable. Someone who forgives every injury at once, before she has even registered that she was wronged, may be showing not generosity but a lack of self-respect, and forgiveness that comes too easily can signal that the forgiver does not believe she was owed anything. A person who is slighted again and again by the same colleague, and who forgives each slight as though nothing had happened, may also be teaching the colleague that such slights cost him nothing, which serves neither of them. The point is only that apology is one route to forgiveness rather than its gatekeeper.
R01-C-06: Moral relativism is often defended as the natural philosophy of a tolerant person. If moral claims are true only relative to the standards of a culture, the argument runs, then no culture is in a position to condemn the practices of another, and the proper attitude towards difference is one of respectful non-interference. The appeal of this reasoning is easy to understand, since much historical cruelty was committed by people who were certain that their own customs embodied universal truth and that this certainty licensed them to remake others by force. Yet the argument has a curious structure. Its conclusion, that we ought to tolerate other cultures, is itself a moral claim, and it is plainly meant to hold universally: the relativist does not think tolerance is required only of cultures that happen to value it. A culture whose standards prized conquest would, by relativist lights, be acting rightly when it conquered. If relativism is true, the most a tolerant culture can say to such a culture is that tolerance is valued here, which is a report about itself rather than a reason addressed to anyone else. The relativist who wants tolerance to bind everyone has quietly helped himself to a non-relative principle. None of this shows that relativism is false, and the defender has a reply. Perhaps the claim is not that relativism entails tolerance but that believing it tends to produce tolerant people, by weakening the confidence that fuels crusades. That may be true as a matter of psychology, though the historical record is mixed; doubt can make people gentle, but it can also leave them unable to object to anything at all. More importantly, the reply changes the subject. It defends relativism as a useful belief rather than a true one, and it concedes that the case for tolerance must be made on other grounds. Those other grounds are not hard to find. One can hold that some moral claims are true for everyone and still think that humility about one's own judgements, respect for people's capacity to govern their own lives, and the dismal record of forced conversion all count strongly against intervention in most cases. Such a view is less comfortable than relativism, because it obliges one to say that some practices are wrong even while declining to stamp them out. But it has the advantage of being able to explain why tolerance matters, which relativism, for all its tolerant intentions, cannot.
R01-C-07: Talk of moral progress makes many people uneasy. It sounds like the self-congratulation of every age that has looked back on its predecessors and found them wanting, and it seems to require a fixed standard against which the direction of change could be measured, a standard that is itself in dispute. Yet it is hard to describe the abolition of legal slavery, or the end of public torture as a form of entertainment, merely as changes in fashion, as though they were on a par with a shift in the length of coats. Most people who doubt the idea of moral progress in theory find themselves unable to give it up in particular cases. One influential way of making sense of the idea is to describe progress as the expansion of a circle of concern. Early moral codes, on this telling, extended full consideration only to kin or to members of the tribe; over time the boundary has been pushed outward, to strangers, to foreigners, to people of other races and faiths, and, more recently and more contentiously, to animals. Progress consists in recognising as morally considerable those whom we previously ignored. The picture is appealing because it gives progress a direction without requiring agreement on a complete moral theory: one needs only the modest premise that arbitrary exclusion is a mistake. It also explains why reformers have so often described their work as opening the eyes of their contemporaries rather than changing their values: the values, on this telling, were already present, and only their application had been blocked. The picture is not wrong, but it is incomplete in a way that matters. Some of the clearest cases of progress involve not who counts but what we owe to those who already counted. The view that a husband may beat his wife was not, in most societies that held it, a view that wives fell outside moral concern; wives were very much inside the circle, assigned a place in it that we now regard as degrading. Reform came not from widening the boundary but from revising the terms within it. The same is true of changing attitudes to children, who have always been objects of intense concern, and whose treatment has nonetheless been transformed. There is also a danger in the circle image that its admirers tend to overlook. If progress is measured by the width of the circle, then any extension looks like an advance, and any contraction like a regression. But concern can be extended in ways that are themselves harmful: the circle of a missionary empire was wide, and that width was part of its justification for interfering in other people's lives. Inclusion that comes with a presumption of authority over the included is not obviously better than the indifference it replaces. What matters is not only that more beings are counted, but how they are counted. None of this means that we should abandon the idea of moral progress. It means that progress is less like a single line along which societies advance and more like a series of corrections, each prompted by the discovery that some practice depended on a mistaken belief, an unexamined interest or a failure of imagination. Such corrections can be recognised as improvements without a finished theory of the good, in the way that a scientist can recognise an error without possessing the final truth. That is a more modest claim than the circle image offers, but it is also harder to dismiss as the vanity of the present.
R01-C-08: Virtue ethics asks not what rule an action follows or what outcome it produces but what kind of person performs it. Its central concepts are traits of character such as honesty, courage and compassion, conceived as stable dispositions that lead a person to act well across a wide range of circumstances. The compassionate person does not help only when it is convenient or when someone is watching; her compassion shows itself in the market and at home, towards friends and towards strangers. It is this breadth that distinguishes a virtue from a habit, and it is what makes the attribution of a virtue a substantial claim about a person rather than a summary of what she happened to do last week. In recent decades a group of critics, often called situationists, has argued that this picture is empirically naive. They point to a body of experimental work in social psychology, some of it now disputed, which has been taken to show that small and morally irrelevant features of a situation, such as whether a person is in a hurry or in a pleasant mood, predict whether she will help someone in need far better than anything we know about her character. If behaviour is driven so heavily by circumstance, the critics conclude, then broad traits of the kind virtue ethics requires are rare or nonexistent, and a theory built around them describes a psychology that human beings do not have. On this view, to call someone honest or kind is less a discovery about her than a story we tell to make her conduct look more orderly than it is. The argument is more damaging to some versions of virtue ethics than to others. If the theory claimed that most people possess the virtues, the evidence would tell heavily against it. But the classical tradition never claimed this. It held that full virtue is difficult, uncommon and achieved, if at all, through long training, and that most people are a mixture of good impulses and weak resolve. Evidence that ordinary people are easily swayed by circumstance is exactly what such a tradition would predict. Indeed, much of the advice it offers, to avoid temptations rather than trust oneself to resist them and to choose one's companions with care, makes sense only on the assumption that character is fragile. This reply, however, has a cost that its defenders do not always acknowledge. If genuine virtue is so rare that experimental samples almost never contain it, then virtue ethics can no longer claim the advantage it has often advertised over its rivals: that it describes moral life as it is actually lived, in terms of real people and their recognisable qualities. An ideal that almost no one embodies may still be worth pursuing, but it begins to look less like a description of character and more like a rule of the kind the theory set out to replace, a standard against which conduct is measured rather than a source from which it flows. The situationist challenge, then, does not refute virtue ethics, but it changes what the theory can coherently promise. The theory can keep its account of the ideal, or its claim to realism about ordinary people, but it is hard to see how it can keep both. Which it should give up is a question that experiments alone cannot answer, since it depends on what we want an ethical theory to do: to guide those who aspire to goodness, or to describe those whose characters are already formed.
